title: Knitro: An Integrated Package for Nonlinear Optimization
contribution: Describes Knitro 5.0. The package integrates two interior-point algorithms (a line-search primal-dual method with a trust-region fallback, and a trust-region projected-CG method) and an SLQP active-set method. They share a projected-CG kernel, update the penalty parameter at every iteration, reduce automatically on special problem classes, and offer the first interior-to-active crossover in a nonlinear code.
problem_entry: The user's dilemma: no algorithm guarantees success, and each lives in its own package with a steep learning curve; integrated LP/MIP packages are the model (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Integrate complementary algorithms around shared modules: Interior/Direct with a trust-region fallback on inertia and step-length diagnostics, Interior/CG with a slack-scaled trust region, and SLQP active-set; add crossover and automatic special-case reduction (pp. 3-22).
assumptions: f, c_E, c_I twice continuously differentiable (p. 2); local minimizers near the user's x0 (p. 19); G positive definite on the null space for PCG, Steihaug termination otherwise (pp. 16-17); LP/QP structure must be declared by the user (p. 20).
proof_devices: No theorems; convergence cited: penalty update '[4]' (p. 15), Interior/CG [3, 6] (p. 6), Interior/Direct [38] (p. 5)
Inertia condition (3.6) implies descent for the merit function (p. 5)
sigma switch (3.18) guarantees a negative directional derivative (p. 11)
Projected CG equals reduced CG on Z^T G Z preconditioned by Z^T D Z, so no null-space basis is needed (p. 17)
Infeasibility heuristic from [3]: A_E^T c_E -> 0, A_I^T c_I^- -> 0 (p. 20)
Crossover LP radius (7.22) excludes the inactive constraints if the active-set estimate is correct (p. 22)
experiments: none (no numerical results; only experience claims: merit-function tolerance, p. 5, and cheap warm-started penalty LPs, p. 15)
positioning: Surveys Snopt, FilterSQP, Minos, Lancelot, Conopt, Loqo, Barnlp, Ipopt, Mosek and Pennon (p. 2). Differs from line-search IPMs that modify the Hessian (p. 6), from fixed-penalty rules (p. 14), and from all nonlinear interior codes on crossover (p. 20). Answers the merit-function critics with the filter authors' own table (p. 5).
writing: Figure first (p. 3), boxed algorithms (pp. 7-21), a one-sentence reason for each choice (p. 6); explicit hedges ('inevitably incomplete', pp. 3-4; 'not known at present', p. 5); no conclusion (the paper ends on p. 22).
limits_future: Cannot distinguish an infeasible problem from an infeasible stationary point (p. 20); initial-point strategy only in Interior/Direct (p. 19); D = I preconditioner, with banded and incomplete Cholesky preconditioners for future releases (p. 17); a DIRECT active-set option foreseen (p. 3); no numerical evidence.

method_links.note: Integrates interior and active-set algorithms with crossover, on the LP/MIP analogy; 'both be needed in the years to come'
The undecided barrier rule is exposed as a user option; failure modes (infeasibility, preconditioning) are listed; S105 takes up the preconditioner promise

The primal-dual line-search engine is kept; explicit diagnostics (inertia, step length < alpha_min) trigger a trust-region fallback rather than a repaired component; the SLQP penalty update is the early form of steering
The received view that nonsmooth merit functions interfere with fast progress is contested with experience and the rival's own table, not with a dedicated test

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Special-case reduction as a design requirement
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The general solver must reduce automatically to trust-region Newton-CG (unconstrained), Levenberg-Marquardt (equations) and simplex (LP); S105 then benchmarks against specialists on bounds
Merit-function tolerance is supported by Table 2 of Waechter and Biegler, a paper of the filter school

transferable: Require a general solver to reduce automatically to the accepted special-purpose method on each simple class, and say so in the paper (pp. 19-20)
Use one shared projected-CG kernel with a constraint preconditioner; reuse its factorization for the normal step, the multipliers and an initial feasible point (pp. 15, 17)
Trigger a trust-region fallback on cheap explicit diagnostics (inertia count, small step length) instead of modifying the Hessian (pp. 5-7)
Crossover: a tolerance-based active-set estimate and one EQP step first; if that fails, an LP with radius min c_i/||grad c_i|| over the inactive constraints and nu0 = 10||(y,z)||_inf (pp. 21-22)

coauthors: Richard H. Byrd, Richard A. Waltz

quotes.text: We prefer to revert to a trust region iteration because this permits us to compute a step using a null-space approach, without modifying the Hessian
Although crossover techniques have received much attention in the context of linear programming [27], to the best of our knowledge, none of the nonlinear interior codes provide an option for it.

title: An interior algorithm for nonlinear optimization that combines line search and trust region steps
contribution: Knitro-Direct: a primal-dual line-search interior method that falls back to a globally convergent trust-region CG step when the inertia, step-to-boundary or backtracking tests fail. It hands state explicitly between the two kinds of step, updates the penalty parameter from a model decrease, and couples the barrier and NLP tolerances. On 968 CUTEr problems it matches Knitro-CG, and it is faster where CG is costly.
problem_entry: Line-search IPMs must handle nonconvex models and rank deficiency, and each code does so differently; Knitro-CG is expensive on ill-conditioned Hessians; line-search iterations are known to converge to non-stationary points (pp. 1-4).
key_idea: Always try the direct-factorization step first. If neig > l+m, the step to the boundary is too short, or backtracking fails (imax = 3), switch to trust-region CG steps, handing over Delta = 2 alpha ||d|| and alpha_T = min(1/2, Delta/||d||) (pp. 4-12).
assumptions: f, h, g twice continuously differentiable (p. 2); exact or quasi-Newton Hessians (p. 1); A of full rank for the L-BFGS inversion, else trust-region fallback (p. 13); no assumptions are stated for convergence.
proof_devices: No theorem; global convergence asserted 'similar to' FilterSQP and Knitro (p. 4)
Penalty rule (3.5)-(3.8): D phi <= -rho nu ||c||, which fails if sigma = 1 under negative curvature (p. 7)
Tolerance coupling (3.16)-(3.21): the barrier test implies the NLP test; mu_min = min(eps_opt, eps_feas)/100 (pp. 11-12)
Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury for compact L-BFGS in the primal-dual matrix (p. 13)
experiments: Knitro-Direct vs Knitro-CG (the group's own previous release) on 968 CUTEr problems; 15 min or 3000 iterations counted as failure, tolerance 1e-6. Log2 profiles over evaluations (all problems) and CPU (the 420 with n+m >= 1000). Trust-region steps in 22.9% of iterations (15.9% for negative curvature). L-BFGS close to dense BFGS; exact Hessian solved 788 problems, L-BFGS 693. No external codes (pp. 14-17).
positioning: Credits Loqo for convexification (p. 2); an alternative to the Hessian modification of Barnlp, Ipopt and Loqo (p. 4); answers the failures of Waechter-Biegler [26] and Byrd-Marazzi-Nocedal [7] (p. 4); rejects superlinear mu rules as hard to tune (p. 10); the nu rule comes from El-Hallabi [13] (p. 6).
writing: Numbered 'two reasons' for design choices (pp. 4, 6); parameters given inline, 'In our tests we choose' (pp. 4-12); convergence promised (p. 2) but given only by analogy (p. 4); notation slip alpha_z^max vs alpha_lambda^max (pp. 5, 8); no conclusion.
limits_future: Direct is slower when factorization dominates or negative curvature is frequent (p. 15); quasi-Newton versions less robust (693 vs 788 solved, p. 17); the FD option is costly in CPU if gradients are expensive (p. 17); no external comparison, no future-work section.

method_links.note: The classical primal-dual engine is kept; explicit diagnostics trigger a trust-region recovery path for that iteration; the repair is a fallback with a radius hand-off, not a component change
Two complementary step computations in a unified algorithmic and software framework
The rival's idea is credited (Loqo); known external failure examples are answered with a design
The baseline is the group's own previous release, not a rival code; shared components control implementation effects; CPU only for n+m >= 1000
In this paper, global convergence of the implemented hybrid is asserted by analogy, not analysed

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Inner (barrier) tolerances are chosen so that inner success implies outer (NLP) success, with no oversolving; the floor on mu comes from the NLP tolerances
The nu rule, 'inspired by trust region methods', was adopted for efficiency; S042 derives it from its steering guidelines afterwards (pp. 18-20)

transferable: Hand state between step types: Delta = 2 alpha ||d|| after a line-search step; first backtrack min(1/2, Delta/||d||) after a trust-region step; stay with trust-region steps after a rejected one (pp. 8, 12)
Couple the inner and outer tolerances: eps_mu = max(theta mu, eps - mu), mu_min = min(eps_opt, eps_feas)/100 (pp. 10-12)
Scale the stopping tests by max(1, ||grad f||_inf) and by the initial infeasibility, and state which invariances each factor buys (pp. 9-10)
Try a second-order correction only when the rejection is due solely to constraint growth, reusing the factorization (pp. 8-9)
On a singularity message, raise the pivot tolerance from 1e-8 by factors of 10 up to 0.5; apply at most five iterative-refinement steps (p. 12)
Report the trigger shares of a safeguard and the internal time shares behind CPU differences (pp. 15-16)
coauthors: Richard A. Waltz, Jose Luis Morales, Dominique Orban

quotes.text: In this paper we describe a mechanism for stabilizing the line search iteration that is different from those proposed in the literature.
We use instead the following simple strategy for updating µ that has performed as well in our tests as have more complicated superlinear rules.

title: Steering exact penalty methods for nonlinear programming
contribution: Generalizes the SLQP penalty update into guidelines that set the penalty parameter against the best attainable progress in linearized feasibility, measured by an auxiliary LP with nu = infinity. Implements them in Knitro-Active, relates them to normal-step trust-region SQP, and derives the line-search merit rule of Knitro-Interior/Direct from them.
problem_entry: Sl1QP-type methods never reached production software, which the authors conjecture is due to the penalty choice; two toy examples show that too small a nu fails and that no fixed nu works from every start; multiplier-based and huge-nu rules fail too (pp. 2-7).
key_idea: Steer nu by an auxiliary LP (nu = infinity): reach linear feasibility if attainable, else a fraction eps1 of the best reduction; then impose the margin condition (5.14), model decrease >= eps2 nu times the feasibility gain (pp. 8-11).
assumptions: f, h, g twice continuously differentiable (p. 3); exact penalty theory, nu > ||lambda*||_inf near regular solutions (p. 7); in Section 7, W positive definite on the null space and equality constraints only (pp. 18-19).
proof_devices: Two one-dimensional counterexamples with plots: the penalty function is monotone for nu < 1; for any nu there is no decreasing path from some start (pp. 6-8)
The examples revisited under Algorithm 5.1: nu > 3 x_k^2/(1 - eps2) enlarges the basin of attraction (pp. 13-14)
Descent derivation (7.28) => (7.31), invalid if sigma = 1 and d^T W d < 0 (pp. 19-20)
Theory by inclusion: the implemented condition (5.14) implies the weaker condition analysed in [7] (p. 13)
experiments: ADLITTLE: the fixed-nu failure is reproduced; Knitro-Active raises nu to 1e4 and solves it in 1 iteration (Delta0 = 1e10) or 6 (Delta0 = 10) (p. 15). Huge-nu ablation on 616 CUTEr problems: 485 solved -> 449 (nu = 1e5) -> 321 (nu = 1e10) (pp. 15-16). Extra LPs < 3% of simplex iterations (p. 13). The headline efficiency claims come without tables (pp. 13, 20).
positioning: Extends [6]. Set against Fletcher's Sl1QP practice, multiplier-based rules, and Chen-Goldfarb and Leyffer et al. (who do not assess nu's effect on the step); similar to but distinct from Yuan. Recasts Byrd-Omojokun, Powell-Yuan and Celis-Dennis-Tapia as the same kind of relaxation. Cites Waechter's critique and his controlled comparison (pp. 2-20).
writing: Three-stage history (p. 2); headline 'ceases to be a heuristic' (p. 1); conjecture flagged as such (p. 5); guidelines in words, then inequalities, then an algorithm (pp. 9-11); examples revisited (pp. 13-15); candid admission that penalty SQP is untested (p. 11); an open question and three-sentence final remarks (p. 20).
limits_future: Penalty SQP not implemented, so its trade-offs are unknown (p. 11); extension to penalty line-search methods is open (p. 20); the variant needs eps1 -> 1 for a fast rate (p. 11); the main efficiency claims are unreported (pp. 13, 20).

quotes.text: The following example shows that it is not possible to prescribe in advance a value of the penalty parameter that is adequate at every iteration.
We conclude that the risks of using excessively large penalty parameters are real indeed and that an adaptive strategy, such as the one described above is valuable in practice.

title: A numerical study of active-set and interior-point methods for bound constrained optimization
contribution: Benchmarks Knitro's SLQP and two interior methods against the gradient-projection specialists TRON and L-BFGS-B (and SNOPT) on 29 large bound-constrained CUTEr problems. Finds SLQP weaker at identifying the active set and CG preconditioning decisive, and designs incomplete Cholesky preconditioners for SLQP and for the barrier interior method.
problem_entry: Mature interior-point and active-set methods make it 'an appropriate time to evaluate'; bound constraints are chosen to remove degeneracy, isolate ill-conditioning and face a strong specialist (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Compare like with like (both interior codes inside Knitro; quasi-Newton codes in a separate section), explain the profiles with internal counters, then build incomplete Cholesky preconditioners on the reduced Hessian and on the condensed system (pp. 2-17).
assumptions: f smooth, bounds l <= u (p. 2); G positive definite on the null space, with trust-region and negative-curvature features ignored in the preconditioning analysis (pp. 9-10); central-path approximation Lambda ~ mu S^-1 behind mu S^-2 (p. 14).
proof_devices: No theorems; equivalence of TRON's reduced CG and preconditioned projected CG (p. 11)
Block elimination (9) -> (10) -> (11), enabling incomplete Cholesky of grad^2 L + A_I^T D_s A_I (p. 13)
Dimension count n - t_k vs n, shown to explain only part of the CG gap (pp. 7-8)
Trust-region shape analysis (14) vs (15) and distortion of the barrier stop test, explaining cvxbqp1 (pp. 16-17)
experiments: Table 1: 29 problems (n 2000-100000), TRON 1.2 and Knitro 5.0 Direct/CG/Active at defaults, 10000-iteration limit; reports iter, feval, CPU, aveCG, endCG/n and failure codes, with profiles. Table 2: a MATLAB Knitro/CG on 7 small problems x 9 preconditioner options (e.g. total CG 3962 -> 44). Table 3: SNOPT, L-BFGS-B and the three Knitro codes with L-BFGS m = 20 (pp. 4-20).
positioning: The Gould et al. survey is the map (p. 1); remedies point to the Byrd-Waltz parametric-LP SLQP [6] (p. 8); incomplete Cholesky from Lin-More [14] (p. 7); no external interior codes run, defended as controlling implementation effects (p. 3).
writing: The abstract leads with the authors' own method losing (p. 1); observations under run-in heads, each with a mechanism (pp. 7-8); hedges 'we speculate' (p. 16) and 'more research is needed' (p. 8); ends with an 'In summation' paragraph (p. 20).
limits_future: Preconditioning tested only in a MATLAB prototype on n <= 324 (p. 14); incomplete Cholesky results for Knitro/Active deferred (p. 11); stopping tests left at defaults (p. 4); bounds only. Future: SLQP active-set identification (p. 8) and improved quasi-Newton updating (p. 20).

quotes.text: We have chosen the two interior-point methods available in the knitro package, as opposed to other interior-point codes, to minimize the effect of implementation details.
The use of preconditioning has helped bridge the gap in the exact Hessian case, but in the quasi-Newton case, improved updating procedures are clearly needed for general purpose methods.
